So we use a LB block (Assign MAC) to tell the ESP32 which to pair to which cube slot (1 or 2). Running a program and after program finishes or is stopped, does not disconnect anything. The cubes pairing with the ESP will remain until the ESP is powered off or the Cubes are powered OFF... Maybe after a certain delay the ESP is not communicating with LB, it will disconnect the cubes? posts.text: There are few modes (5) for the Handset. I used mode 0 (RCKEY). Pressing 2 or 3 keys on the same side will report only ONE key pressed. However, in mode 0, pressing one key on side A, and one key on side B at the same time will report correctly the 2 keys pressed. posts.text: @Bliss I tested now 3 ESP32 VROOM Devkit 1 boards, from 2 different manufacturers. What works is discovering the devices in the BT control program of Win11. It is discovered as "CCubes_ESP32_Bridge". I press connect, Win11 says OK. Then I start up the latest LEGO Blockly version either in the Chrome browser from your website or the updated stand-alone versions. Then I select the "C.Cube ESP Bridge" and press "connect". The dialog window comes up and shows only one item, "CCubes_ESP32_Bridge (coupled)". I select that item and press connect and immediately the "Connection cancelled or device not responding" error message is shown. At this point, no COM port is shown in the "Advanced settings/COM tab". Hmmm, I can't remember how that worked. OK - I removed the discovered "CCubes_ESP32_Bridge" item from the BT manager, back to LEGO Blockly, same procedure, "CCubes_ESP32_Bridge (coupled)" is still in the available device list, press connect and - WORKS. On all three ESP boards. They don't show up in the Win11 BT manager, nor in the COM port list, as all other ESPs for Int.A - I guess this is how it should be right? Best Thorsten

posts.text: I doubt that. CaDA always credits the designers on the box with their name and signature (bottom right corner). The Mercedes-AMG GT3 has no name or signature on the box, so far it's been a mystery to me who designed it. The instructions (page 25: "Developers' Approach") only mention "CaDA R&D" and "CaDA Team". So I'm guessing it was an in-house project, or maybe they preferred anonymity. I can't say much about the Audi RS6 specifically since I haven't built it, nor have I seen its instructions. In general, I've always found CaDA's instructions pretty good. LEGO's are often a bit more clear, but even LEGO had times they made choices for instructions that couldn't be worse. The "color vomit" in LEGO models (the use of many different unrelated colors in places "assumed" out of sight) helps a lot to simplify things too. Personally I hate that and am really glad CaDA sticks with proper color accuracy and subtlety for things like pins, axles, connectors, and anything underneath the visible outside shell. I'd say there's nothing wrong with a beginner trying their hands on a complex model, as long as they're aware what they're getting into. Best is to just take your time and enjoy the journey. If you try to rush to the finish line, mistakes easily sneak in and cause a lot of frustration to track down. On the other hand, starting first with smaller and simpler builds gets a person acquainted with more and more techniques and parts, making it easier to spot potential mistakes or just understand how something goes together even if the instructions feel shortcoming.

posts.title: 18+ helicopter wishlist
posts.text: An absolute, unequivocal YES to this from me! I've been waiting an eternity for a large LEGO Technic flagship set that is not a ground vehicle. Unfortunately, this is extremely unlikely to occur anytime soon, and the LEGO 42145 Airbus H175 Rescue Helicopter is indeed the closest set we have at the moment, but for certain I would definitely and immediately buy any large-scale aircraft of this magnitude and complexity if LEGO ever chose to release such a set. Ideally, it would be nice for such a set to be unlicensed - and even if it that means it wouldn't be a conventional helicopter, a futuristic wing-in-ground-effect vehicle, eVTOL aircraft, or some vehicle of that nature with lift-fan proprotors could use very similar swashplate and blade-pitch mechanisms as a conventional helicopter model would, perhaps enclosed in a shroud of some kind. The proprotor pitch-control mechanism could employ a similar design as the rotor head in the Airbus H175, reusing the special elements created for that set. However, because you mentioned that the set would have an 18+ label, that usually implies the set would be licensed, which makes sense for a flagship. Therefore, a more realistic model that fits this label could be based off of an electric vertical takeoff-and-landing (eVTOL) aircraft of some sort, probably a licensed one like a Joby S4 or Archer Midnight. Again, the same special rotor head and swashplate elements created for the H175 could be employed again here as the blade-control mechanisms on all of the aircraft's proprotors, which would also tilt 90 degrees to transition between vertical takeoff and horizontal flight modes. Realistically, it is possible that such a set could be released within the next 3-4 years as global certification processes conclude on upcoming commercial eVTOL air taxis. Here in the United States, the Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) is currently on track to award the first type-certificates for Joby and Archer eVTOL aircraft over the next two years, with commercial service expected by the Summer 2028 Olympic Games in Los Angeles, CA. Europe's aviation safety regulator (EASA) is expected to approve these aircraft shortly thereafter. Once certified, these aircraft will enter commercial service and, absent any major incidents, should enough go according to plan, LEGO may then explore options for creating a Technic set based on an eVTOL aircraft. The best news of all for eVTOLs is that because they are officially civil aircraft, LEGO will now have another opportunity to explore vertical flight in Technic sets without running the risk of military association, as they did with the cancelled 42113 V-22 Osprey set back in 2020. While it is true that eVTOL aircraft too will also have military applications, they will be primarily intended and certified for civil operation and will effectively join most past conventional airplane and helicopter designs (like Airbus' helicopters) as multipurpose airframes, which will make it impossible for any organization to argue that LEGO is violating it's "no military" rule by creating VTOL aircraft, as they demonstrated with the 42181 VTOL Heavy Cargo Spaceship set back in 2024. While this is only just a theory for now, I do believe that an eVTOL aircraft or some other hybrid aircraft is far more likely to get the flagship slot than a conventional helicopter, in part because anything approaching the size of Jeroen Ottens' large helicopter MOC would likely not pass LEGO's durability testing, at least without many massive, expensive new parts and cumbersome reinforcement that would render the whole model unwieldy. At least with an eVTOL aircraft, there are wings and other components and functions beyond just the fuselage and rotors that justify the large parts count. posts.text: @ShaydDeGrai same here: Thank you very much! As you may know, we have a new forum on EB, the Vintage Robotics forum. Matching threads and posts in the Technic Forum (or elsewhere) are currently being split/moved to that forum (with user permission only of course). As you also know it all began with TLG's Interface A, which is just a "dumb" TTL to 4V/high amp driver in addition to a two-sensor signal shaper, providing TTL signals. I/O was done via parallel type interfaces, either already built into the 8/16 bit computers of the pre-1990's or via a dedicated ISA bus card. Text oriented programming was required; LOGO, COMAL, BASIC, PASCAL, C were compatible programming languages. Then came Control Lab (or Interface B) - and programming LEGO machines became graphical. This was as early as 1993, if I recall correctly. And then the CodePilot, and eventually Mindstorms. Even the RIS system 1.0 (RCX) came with a "blockly" programming environment (which is so hyped nowadays), perfectly suited for the younger students. The NXT went BT, had strongly increased computing power, but still, line followers were one major fun thing (since the turtle days of LOGO) in the curricula. I personally stopped it then, no EV3 here or SPIKE, or whatnot. I have to admit, that I went into PoweredUp for mainly one reason: Motors with rather precise rotation encoders, and built-in PID capability in the hubs. Throughout these years, I was thinking: How do the schools and even universities raise all the money? TLG made new systems almost always incompatible to their predecessors (the 9V line lived quite some time and in multiple LEGO worlds). If they wanted to keep up - a) good amounts of money were needed, and b) highly motivated teachers willing to learn before they could teach. The accompanying material, e.g., for the pre-1990 Technic Control curricula is (still today - no nostalgia involved here!), is a blast. Well, now I know firsthand, that my doubts were justified. Again, thank you for sharing your observations and thoughts! All the best Thorsten

posts.title: So, what Do people want?
posts.text: As a former educator who still has a lot of personal connections to the field, I can tell you that there are a LOT of school systems and summer camp programs that are extremely unhappy with The Lego Group right now. Many of these programs don't have a lot of resources to begin with and they invested heavily in MindStorms and Spike (parts, curriculum design, tutorials, tie-in projects to other courses, etc). TLG killed off both of those and, at least as far as most US STEM-related k-12 educators are concerned, have offered nowhere near a decent replacement. I spoke with one teacher whom I'd worked with on the development of RoboLab. He told me flat out that if Lego never invested another dime in anything other than keeping the existing software running on current versions of iOS and Android for Spike (which they plan to do for the next 5 years) and just kept cranking out the same classroom kit they've been selling for years now (nope - no new spare parts, just spending down existing inventory), he'd be happy (he is very much not, right now, BTW). If they'd do the same for Mindstorms he'd be ecstatic. He has no use for PowerUp, Control+ or anything electronic that they've done recently. The current CS&AI kits offer little beyond what he was doing with PIC chips, LabView and 9v Technic Motors thirty years ago; it's just nicer packaging with a Python front end (which he actually dislikes - assembly language programming offered more teachable moments leading to a better understanding of what was really happening under the hood). To hear him vent, he claims that TLG took what should be a 3rd grader experience, dumbed it down even further and repackaged it as a high school program so kids who slept through science and math could feel good about their (lack of real) "STEM mastery". TLG had a really good thing going with Mindstorms and SPIKE and a lot of kids benefited from the curricula they enabled; the death of those two lines has forced once loyal customers to resort to cheap clone parts just to keep their labs running (nothing lasts forever, kids trying to reverse drive a worm gear do a job on even high quality motors - "professor, why is my robot making a funny smell?"). Even school systems that can afford to update their labs (as many did during MindStorm's various generations) are now looking elsewhere given the limited/dumbed-down nature of the current line of "smart" bricks/controllers compared to the power and flexibility of stuff they were shipping a decade ago.

posts.title: Hello!
posts.text: Hi everyone, Ricardo from the Netherlands here! I just joined Eurobricks, so I thought I'd start by saying hello. My LEGO hobby has taken a bit of a digital turn: I rebuild official LEGO sets brick by brick in Mecabricks and record the whole build as a timelapse. Architecture, Icons, Technic, Speed Champions, Star Wars... pretty much anything that catches my eye. It's a great way to "build" sets I don't own, including retired ones I'll probably never get my hands on. A few months ago I decided to start sharing these builds, so I started a YouTube channel and a small website to keep track of everything. I'm at around 30 build videos now and still learning a lot along the way, especially about getting colors and details right when the digital parts library doesn't have everything. I'm also planning to start streaming my builds live on Twitch soon. I build websites for a living, so making the site myself was half the fun. I'm mostly here to learn from all the knowledgeable builders on this forum, talk about new sets, and pick up some tips on digital building. Which sets would you love to see built digitally? posts.title: Do you think in chinese. how to get into that habit if you don't have enough vocabulary
posts.text: I had the advantage of learning Chinese while in China, completely immersed from day one. And I forced myself to interact with local people a lot every day, so things like this rapidly got "smoothed out." What I found was that if I used clumsy, awkward or round-about language to say simple things outside, in real life, the people I was talking with would spontaneously correct me without even thinking about it. "Oh, you mean..." I also had the benefit of nearly always having one or more native teachers, either paid or volunteers, who would straighten out most of my bad speech habits immediately and mercilesssly. Not with scholarly grammar rule explanations, just with "It's more natural to say it like this: xyz 123, etc."

posts.title: Do you think in chinese. how to get into that habit if you don't have enough vocabulary
posts.text: Hi! My experience is that after a massive amount of input, I will often "hear Chinese voices in my head". I.e., the transition starts on its own. Entire sentences that I could readily use. Other learners may have different experiences, though. Famous polyglots, such as Kató Lomb, describe self-talk (she used the term autolog) as an important part of the process of learning the language to a professional level. She shares that she used this almost from the outset (other polyglots also advocate doing this from the beginning, e.g., Benny Lewis). However, my current position is that it is best to wait until you have a fairly good grasp of the rhythm of the language, or you have someone to correct you as to avoid fossilizing erroneous patterns. You may force your native language's grammar and rhythm "through a Chinese dictionary."

posts.title: TOCFL (Test of Chinese as a Foreign Language)
posts.text: I would write notes on key details, like dates, times, activities, amounts, restrictions, advantages, disadvantages, etc. It's faster for me to write in Pinyin, so that's mostly how I took notes. After you have done a lot of mock questions, you start to be able to understand what information in the audio recording is going to come up in the question, because they quite awkwardly put it into the dialogue, and the questions tend to be quite similar in structure throughout the exams, so your note taking will get better over time.

posts.title: Do you think in chinese. how to get into that habit if you don't have enough vocabulary
posts.text: abcdefg's self-talk routine above is the real answer to how this gets built, and becky82 is also right that it is a byproduct. They are describing two different stages. The deliberate version is what you use to build the habit. The byproduct version is what it becomes once output turns automatic. Jadexx asked the part that is easy to skip: where to start. You do not need thought vocabulary to begin. You need perception vocabulary. Thinking in Chinese, at the start, is not composing ideas. It is labeling what is already in front of you. 桌上有一个杯子。窗户开着。The grammar will stay broken for months and every sentence will be a baby sentence. That is fine. The exercise is not the sentence, it is the retrieval: meaning to Chinese without passing through English first. A few hundred words is enough to train that. What makes it grow is the routine abcdefg described above, and it runs from day one, because it needs no vocabulary either. When you hit a word you do not have, circle around it in Chinese. The big cold drink. The paper bag by the door. Do not switch to English to find the word. The refusal to switch is the actual skill, and it works at any level. On dreaming, Jadexx, there is no routine. None that anyone has found. It tracks hours of input, not techniques, which is why everyone here who reports it also reports a decade or a bootcamp. Put the self-talk on a schedule, since that is the part you control. The dreams show up when they show up.
